De- spite extensive research, typical spray cooling systems only function effectively within constrained conditions. Therefore, creating a general model for spray cooling is essential for accurately predicting its functionalities. In this work, we employed six machine learn- ing (ML) algorithms to analyze the thermal performance and hydraulic properties of spray cooling. Leveraging data from 25 previous studies encompassing different working fluids, spray atomization types, Reynolds numbers (Re), Nusselt numbers (Nu), and Weber numbers (We), our ML models significantly enhance the prediction of spray cooling functionalities compared to traditional correlations. The effectiveness of these ML algo- rithms was experimentally validated, yielding mean absolute percentage errors (MAPEs) of 6% 20% for Nu and 4% 16% for mean droplet diameter d d, respectively. Then, − − − − we proposed a general correlation for the thermal performances of various working fluids, atomization methods, and operational conditions, achieving a 38% reduction in MAPE compared to the most accurate existing correlation. Subsequently, this general correlation was integrated into the ML models, resulting in MAPEs ranging from 0.48% to 2.3%. Furthermore, we optimized the key factors of spray cooling with the Nu number reaching 220. Finally, we employed SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) approach to interpret the ML models and to identify an optimal strategy towards greatly enhanced thermal performance. This study demonstrates that ML significantly outperforms the empirical correlations for evaluating spray cooling performance and functionalities, paving a new avenue for thermoregulation of modern power systems. Achieving these features relies on generating a sequence of droplets of the appropriate sizes with precise timing and flux. Spray cooling has been applied in both relatively low-temperature applications, like cooling avionic equipment and data centers, and high-temperature applications such as in the alloy industry (Chen et al. 2022). In this respect, the Nu number and its correlations are commonly used for assessing the thermal management potential of a cooling technique in case of single-phase convection. How- ever, the further improvement of spray cooling technology requires overcoming several challenges, including high pressure drops across the nozzle (Nasr et al. 2006), as well as the hydrodynamic and spatial optimization of certain key factors such as the mean droplet diameter d d , mean droplet velocity u m, nozzle-to-surface distance H, nozzle diameter d n, and volumetric flux rate Q. As such, adaptively generating a flux of microdroplets with proper sizes is crucial not only for estimating heat transfer capacity but also for calculat- ing the required pressure drop across the nozzle. Yet, precisely measuring droplet size is a demanding task that requires instantaneous optical measurements via laser scattering and prompt analysis of a large volume of images captured by a high-speed camera. 1.1 Empirical models of spray droplet sizes and thermal performance It is difficult to overemphasize the importance of spray droplet sizes in determining the amount of heat dissipation upon contact with a heated surface. In practical applications, spray dimensions and the required pressure across a nozzle are typically determined accord- ing to the desired droplet size. However, accurately estimating the full spectrum of droplet sizes is highly challenging due to the inherent variability and dynamic instability of the spray emitted from a nozzle. Consequently, researchers often use mean droplet diameter rather than full distributions to characterize droplet sizes in spray systems. Among these, the Sauter mean diameter is one of the most widely used parameter (Pacek et al. 1998). It is defined as the diameter of a droplet whose volume-to-surface area ratio is equivalent to that of the entire spray sample. Several models have been developed to predict mean droplet diameter, varying significantly in terms of complexity, accuracy, and applicability. One of the early models proposed by Bonacina et al. predicted d d based on the pressure differ- ence across the orifice (Bonacina et al. 1979). While this model showed good agreement with nozzle manufacturer data for subcooled Freon-113, its neglect of key fluid proper- ties, such as density and surface tension, resulted in poor generalizability with an MAPE as high as 320% on the consolidated dataset used in this study. In contrast, later studies have improved predictive accuracy by incorporating additional influencing factors, includ- ing key fluid properties, into their models. Estes and Mudawar (Estes and Mudawar 1995) extended earlier models by incorporating additional input variables, including nozzle diam- eter d n , Weber number We, fluid properties, liquid velocity and Reynolds number Re. Their model showed improved accuracy on the consolidated dataset, achieving an MAPE of 92%, and exhibited low prediction errors (MAPE = 12.4%) only within the low-flow range of 0.12 1.65 L/min. Similarly, Nasr et al. further advanced predictive capabilities by − including nozzle-to-surface distance H, enabling their model to handle a broader range of flow rates (0.53–5.89 L/min) and nozzle diameter (0.61 mm < d n < 1.7 mm) (Nasr et al. 1999). This method accounts for droplet size non-uniformity, providing a more comprehensive representation of the spray behavior. However, emerging technologies—such as AI accelerators and next- generation chips—necessitate the thermal management of extremely high heat fluxes while maintaining low device temperatures. This has incurred an urgent need for non-boiling spray cooling systems, where heat transfer is governed by a combination of convection, conduc- tion, and direct evaporation mechanisms. In non-boiling spray cooling systems, the key factors influencing thermal performance include coolant properties, nozzle-to-surface dis- tance, nozzle orifice size, droplet dynamics, and surface temperature (Liang and Mudawar 2017b). Early investigations primarily concentrated on convective heat transfer, developing correlations that relate the Nusselt number (Nu) to the Reynolds (Re) and Prandtl (Pr) numbers. Mudawar and Valentine (Mudawar and Valentine 1989) proposed two empiri- cal correlations for Nu as a function of Re and Pr. Their model applies to cases with flow rates between 0.6 10− 3m3s− 1 and 1.0 10− 3 m3s− 1, and with Pr numbers × × ranging from 2.06 to 6.33. Rybicki and Mudawar (Rybicki and Mudawar 2006) extended Mudawar’s correlation to dielectric fluids, resulting in a broader applicability. Cho and Pon- zel (Cho and Ponzel 1997) enhanced the accuracy of previous models by incorporating the effects of varying nozzle diameters and a broader range of flow rates of 3.7 8.7 ml/s. − However, these convection-based models in the form of Nu = f(Re, Pr) overlook the influence of droplet dynamics. To address this, Hsieh and Tien (Hsieh and Tien 2007) devel- oped a correlation based on the Weber number (We) and droplet diameter, accounting for droplet impact dynamics and droplet size distribution. Their model, developed for refriger- ant R-134a in the single-phase regime, can predict 80% of the experimental Nu numbers within ± 10% uncertainty margin. Several researchers have developed correlations that uti- lize surface diameter as the characteristic length, independent of droplet size. Jiang and Dhir proposed a single-phase correlation with significant errors at high Re values (Jiang and Dhir 2004). Similarly, Oliphant et al. derived a Nu correlation for air-assisted atomizers, demonstrating that spray cooling can outperform jet cooling in heat dissipation while requir- ing significantly less mass flux (Oliphant et al. 1998). Although these models are applicable over wide ranges of Re and Pr numbers, they do not account for the influence of droplet size. More recent studies have gone beyond pure convection by incorporating the effects of direct evaporation at the liquid film surface. The direct evaporation mechanism becomes significant under conditions of low liquid mass flux, high gas pressure, and elevated sur- face temperature. For instance, Wang et al. developed a correlation for Nu number based on Re number and dimensionless temperature (Wang et al. 2010). Additionally, there has been a focus shift toward local heat transfer behaviors rather than the overall performance evaluated by the averaged Nu numbers. Key mechanisms—such as liquid film evolution, droplet impingement, tran- sitions between heat transfer regimes, and localized temperature variations—cannot be fully captured through empirical approaches alone. These underlying processes can instead be investigated more effectively and resource-efficiently using advanced computational fluid dynamics (CFD), which enables detailed exploration of the multiphase interactions and heat transfer phenomena central to spray cooling. Numerical simulations of spray cooling are a cost-effective methodology that allows for detailed investigation of heat transfer mecha- nisms through the controlled isolation of individual parameters. Early studies focused on simulating a single droplet impact on surfaces (Pasandideh-Fard et al. 1996; Pidsley 1983). In these studies, key parameters such as wall temperature and heat flux were monitored for high-temperature spray systems under various wettability conditions (Benther et al. 2021; Liang and Mudawar 2017a). Based on initial single-droplet studies, later investigations have extended to multi-droplet spray scenarios (Pan and Suga 2005). However, managing key parameters in multi-droplet conditions is more challenging due to the complex interac- tions between droplets (Liang et al. 2019; Yang et al. 2024). Although these studies offer qualitative descriptions of thermal efficiency, they encounter challenges in quantifying the heat transfer characteristics of droplet clusters (Yang et al. 2024). Accurate evaluation of spray cooling necessitates the comprehensive understanding of not only droplet behaviors but also their complex interactions with the surrounding. Recent research has incorporated additional heat transfer mechanisms—such as film evaporation, convection, and nucleate boiling—into numerical models to better capture the complexity of the violent process. For example, Jiang et al. (Jiang et al. 2015) simulated the droplet impact on a liquid film at different wall temperatures. Further advancements have been made through the Discrete Phase Model (DPM) technique, enabling more accurate calculation of droplet trajectories (Dinc 2015; Khan 2013). Nevertheless, accurate prediction of spray cooling performance is persistently hindered by the lack of reliable heat transfer correlations. Recent efforts have incorporated high-speed photography (Yang et al. 2024), cylindrical surfaces (Zhang et al. 2024), and multi-nozzle sprays into numerical simulations (Hou et al. 2018). Yet, these stud- ies are often constrained by limited operating conditions—such as constant wall tempera- ture, velocity, and flow rate—and tend to overlook the effects of nozzle types and surface sizes. 1.3 Machine learning in spray technology Machine learning (ML) has revolutionized the approach to studying and analyzing complex engineering problems (Kamrani et al. 2021; Malik et al. 2018; Padhi et al. 2022; Zakeri et al. 1 3 Thermohydraulic performance of spray cooling systems: a general model… Page 7 of 54 29 2024). By employing statistical algorithms, researchers can effectively learn from available and known background data and generalize to unseen scenarios. However, their study was limited to con- stant orifice diameters and was conducted under very low temperature conditions. Chang and Park (Chang and Park 2023) used ML to investigate the characteristics of flash boiling sprays under diverse injection conditions. They compared the results from Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), and XGBoost, confirming the best performance of XGBoost. Deshannavar et al. Their analysis was limited by a small dataset and focused solely on two input features, i.e., spray height and water pressure. Çolak (Çolak 2025) chose wall temperature and We number as the input features in his ANNs model to estimate the spreading coefficient of liquid nitrogen on superheated surfaces, achieving a high determination coefficient R2 of 0.997. Wang et al. (Wang et al. 2019) applied backpropagation neural networks to assess temperature uniformity in near-space vehicles managed by spray cooling. Using environ- mental pressure, nozzle inlet temperature, and flow rate as input parameters, they exclu- sively focused on the flash boiling regime but with much left unexplored. 1.4 Objectives and motivation of this study So far, we have categorized the literature on spray cooling into three main approaches: experimental studies, numerical simulations, and ML techniques. In the following discus- sion, we highlight the major limitations associated with each of these approaches and out- line how this study addresses them through AI-driven methods. Even though experimental studies are valuable for capturing physical behaviors, they often suffer from poor gener- alizability across varying test conditions, geometries, and fluid properties. The empirical models derived from these studies were typically based on a restricted set of input variables from a limited range of working fluids, often neglecting other important factors and key heat transfer mechanisms (Hughes et al. 2021). Moreover, experimental investigations are highly resource-intensive and require substantial time and effort input, making them impractical for rapid design iterations or large-scale optimization. Numerical simulations, while effective in capturing the detailed droplet impact behav- iors, still face significant challenges (Cai et al. 2021). Due to the inextricable coupling of mass, momentum, and energy equations across the continuous phases, discrete phases, and liquid film, these numerical methods demand substantial computational resources, time, and cost. Moreover, accurately capturing the complex evolutions of droplet impact dynam- ics presents persistent challenges, primarily due to the requirement for multiscale meshing 1 3 29 Page 8 of 54 M. S. Lori et al. and the precise tuning of convergence parameters. Additionally, the use of oversimplified boundary conditions or unrealistic assumptions can further compromise the accuracy and reliability of the simulation results (Wan et al. 2023). ML-based approaches have demon- strated considerable potential in thermal analyses but remain underexplored in the context of spray cooling. Most existing ML studies have focused on cooling technologies such as microchannel heat sinks (Kim et al. 2022; Lee et al. 2021; Mohammadpour et al. 2022; Qiu et al. 2021; Shamsoddini Lori 2022), boiling (Rashidi et al. 2022; Sinha et al. 2021; Suh et al. 2024), and condensation (Khodakarami et al. 2024; Thukral et al. 2025). Only a few studies have applied ML to spray technologies, and even fewer ML works have been done specifically for spray cooling systems. These studies typically relied on datasets derived from a single working fluid or a simplified spray configuration, which hinders the develop- ment of a robust and generalized model. Another key challenge in ML is data imbalance when certain operating conditions are underrepresented in the training set, potentially lead- ing to biased predictions (Sami and Sierra 2025). Techniques such as data augmentation and generative adversarial networks (GANs) have been put forward to enrich underrepresented data and improve model robustness. Overfitting is also a common issue, causing models to learn irrelevant patterns and perform poorly on unseen data especially when working with noisy or small datasets. Regularization strategies such as dropout, early stopping, and L1/L2 penalties can help mitigate this issue (Soumare et al. 2021). Furthermore, distribu- tional shift can occur and compromise predictive reliability when deployment conditions differ from those seen during training (Wiles et al. 2021). To address this, advanced sta- tistical methods like continual learning, uncertainty quantification, and multivariate error analysis are being explored to enhance model adaptability in real implementations. Given the limitations on numerical and experimental techniques, it is imperative to explore alter- native ML approaches that can accurately predict heat transfer and hydraulic behaviors over a broad range of input parameters, working fluids, and operating conditions. The thermal performance of spray cooling is governed by a wide range of factors, including volumetric flux rate, fluid properties (e.g., Re and Pr numbers), droplet dynamics (e.g., We number), fluid and surface temperatures, droplet size, and nozzle geometry. In non-boiling spray cool- ing, heat is dissipated through multiple mechanisms such as conduction, film convection, and direct evaporation while droplet impingement facilitates these procedures. Capturing the interplay among these mechanisms is essential for accurate performance prediction and system optimization. However, because of the inherently complex nature of spray cooling, there remains the lack of an effective method to predict and optimize performance based on a comprehensive integration of fluid flow parameters and heat transfer processes. In response to these challenges, this study presents an AI-driven framework that sig- nificantly enhances both the predictive accuracy and generalizability of thermohydraulic behaviors in non-boiling spray cooling systems. A comprehensive dataset from 25 previous experimental spray cooling studies was used to train and validate a range of ML and deep learning (DL) models, namely Decision Tree Regression (DTR), Random Forest Regres- sion (RFR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), Multilinear regression, Multilayer Percep- tron (MLP), and the gradient-boosted model of CatBoost. We employed these models to predict two key performance parameters, i.e., Nusselt number (Nu) and droplet diameter (d d ), across a wide range of operating conditions, fluid properties, nozzle types, and spray configurations. To ensure rigorous and consistent evaluation, these models were appraised using five metrics, namely Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Coefficient of Determination 1 3 Thermohydraulic performance of spray cooling systems: a general model… Page 9 of 54 29 (R2), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and two custom performance indicators (θ and η) which represent the proportions of predictions with the MAPE less than 30% and 50%, respectively. These models were trained on a subset of the data and validated against a deliberately excluded test set to assess their generalization. Regularization tech- niques and hyperparameter tuning were employed to mitigate overfitting and underfitting, while uncertainty quantification and multivariate error analysis were conducted to evaluate model reliability. In addition to these black-box ML approaches, this study introduces a general correlation for spray cooling based on experimental data. The proposed correla- tion aims to capture the combined effects of key variables, including fluid properties, flow rate, droplet dynamics, droplet size, temperature fields, and spray geometrical features. This correlation substantially outperforms traditional empirical methods in terms of predictive accuracy and consistency. The general correlation was then integrated into the ML models to further enhance prediction accuracy. Moreover, the ML and DL models were used in this work to identify optimized geometrical and hydraulic features that maximize the heat transfer coefficient, offering actionable insights for the design and control of advanced spray cooling systems. 2 Data collation Once the variables of interest are determined, the relevant data is gathered from the pub- lished works for ML-based analyses. GBM is an ensemble method that builds a strong predictive model by adding decision trees sequentially. Each new tree is trained to correct the errors of the previous ones, and the process uses gradient descent to minimize a chosen loss function. In regression tasks, this method constructs an additive approximation of the target function by iteratively minimizing the expected value of a loss function such as Mean Squared Error. To improve generalization and prevent overfitting, modern gradient boosting techniques integrate various forms of regularization. Common strategies include shrinkage (reducing the step size of each update), randomization (such as subsampling rows and features), and hyperparameter constraints that limit the complexity of the weak learners (Bentéjac et al. 2021). Over time, GBM has evolved into more efficient and powerful variants, most notably XGBoost, which enhances the original algorithm with key improvements such as regu- larized loss functions, second-order gradient optimization, and built-in support for sparse data. The introduction of regularization into the objective function helps control model complexity and variance reduction during tree construction, thereby improving the training efficiency and the model generalization. XGBoost also introduces row and column subsam- pling, which accelerates training and improves predictive performance by reducing correla- tions among trees. Its sparsity-aware algorithm handles missing and zero values efficiently, further reducing memory usage and the risk of overfitting. LightGBM is primarily optimized for enhancing the training speed and scalability. By employing histogram-based feature binning, the LightGBM algorithm circumvents the need to compute exact loss reductions for every feature value, thereby achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Two novel techniques—Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB)—are central to LightGBM’s performance. GOSS retains all data points with large gradients and randomly samples from those with smaller gradients, preserving the overall gradient distribution while reducing computational cost. EFB reduces dimensionality by combining mutually exclusive features—those that rarely have non-zero values at the same time—into a single feature, effectively avoiding redundancy in high- dimensional sparse datasets. Together, these methods make LightGBM significantly faster than traditional GBM especially on large datasets. CatBoost was recently developed to specifically address the problem of prediction shift (J. T. Hancock & T. M. Khoshgoftaar, 2020a, b). Prediction shift arises when the same data point is used both for computing gradients and making predictions, or when target statistics are derived from the full dataset, leading to target leakage. To resolve this issue, CatBoost introduces two key innovations, namely ordered target statistics and ordered boosting. Ordered target statistics are calculated using only the preceding data points in a randomly permuted training set, ensuring that future information does not leak into the current predic- tions. In ordered boosting, each model is trained only on the subset of the training data that comes earlier in a specific random ordering (permutation) of the dataset, and predictions are made using only preceding trees. These strategies reduce overfitting, increase model robust- ness, and improve generalization, making CatBoost particularly suitable for datasets with categorical features and high variance. 1 3 29 Page 22 of 54 M. By discretizing continuous input features into a fixed number of bins (histograms), HGBT significantly reduces computational and memory overhead. Rather than evaluating every possible split point across all continuous features, the algorithm selects split candidates only from a limited set of bin thresholds, streamlining the tree-building process. This binning strategy allows for faster training and improved scalability without substantial loss in pre- dictive accuracy. Additionally, HGBT implementations typically include native handling of missing values, further enhancing their usability in real-world datasets. While conventional gradient boosting models offer point predictions, they struggle to capture epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. NGBoost was introduced by Duan et al. (Duan et al. 2020) to address this issue. NGBoost extends the gradient boosting framework to probabilistic predictions, modeling a full distribution over the target variable. It does so by minimizing the expected negative log-likelihood (NLL) using natural gradients, which take into account the Rieman- nian geometry of the parameter space. This leads to more stable and efficient convergence compared to standard gradient descent, particularly in complex parameter spaces. Some empirical studies have evaluated and compared the performance of gradient boosting vari- ants in terms of training speed and predictive accuracy. While CatBoost usually demonstrates the highest accuracy particularly in datasets with categorical variables, the differences among those leading implementations are generally marginal (Bentéjac et al. 2021). In terms of training efficiency, LightGBM consistently ranks highest due to its histogram-based optimization and data reduction strategies. Upon impact, spray droplets typically form a thin liquid film on the heated surface. The sys- tem’s cooling performance is then governed by interfacial evaporation, forced convection within the film, and film disruption by incoming droplets in a combined manner. Under conditions of high heat fluxes or elevated surface temperatures, small droplets may have completely evaporated before reaching the surface, accelerating dry-out. Conversely, excessively large spray droplets may accumulate and form a thicker film on the surface, incurring inextricable thermal resistance thereon. Thus, an optimized droplet diameter ensures uniform film coverage without excessive liquid accumulation (Wen-Jei and Clark 1975). Volumetric flux rate Q also strongly influences the liquid film dynamics. At low Q, insufficient liquid replenishment increases the risk of local dry-out (Kim 2007). Increasing Q enhances liquid velocity and promotes convective heat transfer within the film. However, excessive Q can lead to undesirable liquid accumula- tion, which deteriorates thermal performance. Therefore, an optimal Q can balance these competing effects and maintain a sustainable film especially under high heat fluxes. The nozzle-to-surface distance (H) must be likewise tuned to ensure uniform spray distribution and maximize surface coverage. An optimized H improves droplet spreading and rewetting (Guo et al. 2009; Mudawar and Estes 1996). On one hand, spray droplets should have the sufficient momentum to disrupt the liquid film. On the other hand, the impact velocity must be kept below a certain threshold to avoid droplet rebound, which would otherwise lead to poor wetting and enhance dry-out risk (Chen et al. 2018; Kim 2007). Appropriate selection of the nozzle size and inlet pressure, in combination with the optimized values of d d , Q, and H, enables uniform surface wetting and reduces localized dry-out. Spray droplets can coalesce or accumulate upon impact on the heated surface, forming a thin liquid film. Along with droplet impingement, heat is primarily transferred via thin- film convection and evaporation within this film (Xie et al. 2012). It has been reported that spray velocity and volumetric flux rate strongly affect the film thickness. Although liquid film thickness was not explicitly included in our ML datasets, droplet velocity and volu- metric flux rate were incorporated as indirect indicators. At a low volumetric flux rate, the film spreads slowly with relatively weak convection, and droplet impingement dominates heat transfer. At elevated droplet fluxes, however, the increased film velocity enhances thin- film convection (See Fig. 22c). Here, film velocity refers to the speed at which the thin liquid film—formed by coalescing droplets—spreads across the heated surface. Generally, high-velocity impingement stimulates heat transfer by strengthening droplet impact, while an increased flow rate promotes heat dissipation by agitating and thinning the thermal boundary layer (See Fig. 22g and c) (Jiang et al. 2015; Kim 2007). In non-boiling spray cooling, heat transfer is dominated by droplet impingement and thin-film convection particularly under conditions of high mass flux, low ambient gas pressure, and modest surface superheat (Jiang et al. 2015; Jiang and Dhir 2004; Pautsch and Shedd 2006; Xie et al. 2012). In cases of high gas pressure or steep temperature gradients, however, liq- uid film evaporation cannot be neglected. Evaporation occurs as heat is conducted from the surface into the liquid film, while the continuous removal of vapor from the interface allows for sustainable evaporation. The evaporation rate depends primarily on film thickness, the temperature gradient across the film, and the replenishment rate of liquid on the surface. At a fixed temperature gradient, an optimal mass flux is required, that is, it must be sufficient to maintain overall surface wetting while also controlling film thickness to minimize thermal resistance. Deviations from this optimal flux can degrade heat transfer because a lower mass flux may lead to surface dry-out, whereas a higher flux may result in liquid accumulation with extra thermal resistance. Additionally, at constant mass flux and film thickness, increas- ing the temperature gradient promotes thin film evaporation. Maximum heat transfer occurs when the fluid replenishment rate matches the film evaporation rate. However, raising the temperature gradient without adequate liquid supply can induce local dry-out and degrade heat transfer. Therefore, while a thinner liquid film generally correlates with higher heat removal, carefully tuning the spray droplet flux at certain surface temperature is essential to avoid dry-out and maintain efficient cooling (Lustenader et al. 1959). In thin-film evapora- tion, smaller droplets are typically preferred due to their higher surface-to-volume ratio and 1 3 29 Page 48 of 54 M. S. However, under steep temperature gradients, the kinetic energy of small droplets may be significantly reduced—or entirely diminished—by vapor-induced drag force (Neitzel and Dell’Aversana 2002; Xie et al. 2012). To ensure that droplets effectively reach and wet the surface without premature rebound or evaporation, their velocities must be carefully modulated. 5 Conclusions In this paper, we report a general model for spray cooling based on a variety of advanced AI techniques including MLP and CatBoost as well as traditional ML methods such as DTR, RFR, SVR and multiple linear regression. This model involves conducting ML and DL analyses for two types of spray nozzles, namely gas-atomized nozzle and pressure-atomized nozzle. To this end, we focused on two critical thermal and hydraulic parameters of a spray cooling system, i.e., the Nu number and the mean droplet diameter d d. The dataset for AI analyses was curated from 25 prior experimental studies on non-boiling heat transfer in spray cooling. It encompasses a vast amount of data from experiments, involving 12 differ- ent working fluids and various spray atomization methods, conducted under a broad range of testing conditions. To benchmark the performance of these ML and DL protocols, we compared AI predictions with the empirical correlations derived from prior experimental works. In addition, a subset of data points was intentionally excluded as a test set for diverse and robust validation purposes. A general correlation for predicting the Nu number was developed using ML techniques. Compared to traditional empirical correlations, the pro- posed model demonstrates improved prediction accuracy by incorporating a wider range of influential parameters, working fluids, and test conditions. To further enhance heat transfer predictions beyond standalone ML models, the new correlation was integrated into the ML framework. Finally, by combining ML models with advanced optimization techniques, this study identified optimal ranges of hydrodynamic features and spray geometry parameters that can maximize thermal performance. The key findings of this investigation are outlined below. (1) Nu Number Prediction: ML models accurately predict the Nu number with an MAPE of 6% − 20%, RMSE of 2.4–4.95, and R2 of 0.993–0.998. These metrics significantly outperform empirical correlations, which show MAPE of 63% − 435%, RMSE of 17.01–48.28, and R2 of 0.54–0.88. Among ML models, CatBoost achieves the highest accuracy with MAPE = 6%, RMSE = 2.4, R2 = 0.998, followed by RFR with MAPE = 8%, RMSE = 2.91, R2 = 0.996. (2) Droplet Diameter d d Prediction: ML models predict d d with an MAPE of 4% − 16%, RMSE of 0.026–0.115, and R2 of 0.906–0.995, demonstrating substantial improve- ment over empirical correlations with MAPE = 76% − 320%, RMSE = 0.38–0.47, R2 = 0–0.11. CatBoost performs best among ML models with MAPE = 4%, RMSE = 0.026, R2 = 0.995, closely followed by RFR with MAPE = 4%, RMSE = 0.036, R2 = 0.993. (3) Model Validation and Robustness: For the predictions presented in key findings (1) and (2), 20% of the consolidated dataset was randomly reserved as test data for ini- tial validation. To further assess model robustness, a separate subset was intentionally excluded from the training process. On this deliberately excluded data, the ML models 1 3 Thermohydraulic performance of spray cooling systems: a general model… Page 49 of 54 29 consistently predict the Nu number with an MAPE ranging from 9% to 26%, demon- strating superior reliability and generalizability. This work demonstrates the superiority of data-driven approaches in predicting the perfor- mance and evaluating the functionalities of spray cooling systems with an ultra-high effi- ciency and a low computational cost. Nevertheless, the intrinsic black-box nature of these ML and DL models poses challenges in fully understanding how the physical variables within the AI algorithms interact with each other to make predictions. Leveraging ML and DL algorithms, future research should decipher the experimental data by the physical laws of heat and mass transfer so as to insightfully elucidate the underlying mechanisms of spray cooling. In this respect, DL-based computer vision techniques can be applied to monitor droplet morphological evolutions upon impact on the surfaces so that we can investigate how the droplet morphology influences their thermal behaviors during spray cooling. Fur- thermore, we can employ DL to study the complex interactions between impinging droplets and the liquid film formed on the heated surface, pointing to a new avenue for high-effi- ciency thermal regulation of power and energy systems by virtue of thin film evaporation and boiling. JSON: Name: spray_cooling_ml_pipeline Title: Physics-augmented machine learning framework for generalizable prediction and optimization of thermohydraulic performance in non‐boiling spray cooling systems Short Hypothesis: Incorporating a physics-derived Nusselt correlation as an explicit input (correction factor) into machine learning models reduces the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) for predicting Nusselt number in non‐boiling spray cooling by at least 20% relative to equivalent purely data‐driven models trained on the same consolidated dataset. Related Work: Existing approaches to predicting spray cooling performance fall into three categories: empirical correlations, high‐fidelity numerical simulation, and data‐driven models. Empirical correlations (Nu = f(Re,Pr,We,...) or simplified forms) are simple but calibrated to narrow fluids, nozzle types, or flow ranges and fail to generalize across fluids, atomizers, and geometries. CFD and multiphase simulations can resolve droplet‐film interactions but are computationally expensive, require problem‐specific closure models, and are sensitive to meshing and boundary assumptions. Prior ML studies applied standard regressors or neural nets to limited, single‐fluid or small datasets and frequently omit droplet dynamics, nozzle geometry variety, or uncertainty quantification. Reported weaknesses include overfitting on limited regimes, poor extrapolation to unseen nozzle/pressure regimes, inadequate handling of data imbalance and outliers, and lack of interpretable, physics‐consistent outputs. No widely validated, generalizable hybrid (physics + ML) pipeline covering multiple fluids, atomizer types, and operating ranges has been demonstrated. Abstract: Spray cooling offers high heat‐flux removal but current predictive methods are either narrowly calibrated empirical correlations or costly numerical simulations; neither scales to heterogeneous fluids, nozzle types, and operating conditions. We propose a physics‐augmented machine learning pipeline that fuses a data‐derived general Nusselt correlation with ensemble and deep learning regressors to predict both Nusselt number and mean droplet diameter across diverse non‐boiling spray cooling datasets. The pipeline consolidates multi‐study experimental data, performs standardized preprocessing and feature engineering, fits a general correlation via automated optimization, and embeds the correlation as an explicit physics feature for ML models. Contributions include: (1) a reproducible consolidated dataset and preprocessing recipe; (2) an optimized general Nu correlation spanning multiple fluids and atomizers; (3) a physics‐augmented ML workflow with uncertainty estimation and interpretability (SHAP); and (4) a documented experimental protocol for model validation and optimization of spray parameters. Expected outcomes are substantially reduced predictive error, quantified uncertainty bounds, and actionable parameter ranges for improved spray cooling design. Experiments: Datasets: consolidated experimental dataset assembled from 25 published studies (N≈1035 samples) covering multiple working fluids (water, R134a, FC‐series, HFE, PF, PAO, PSF), both pressure and gas atomizers, and ranges: Re∈[0.03,110], Nu∈[0.4,237], dd∈[0.015,2] mm, Q∈[0.3·10−3,142·10−3] mm3·mm−2·s−1, H∈[2.3,600] mm. Preprocessing: standard null handling, StandardScaler for continuous features, LabelEncoder for categorical atomizer/type, calculation of derived features (Re, Pr, We, Td). Train/Test split: stratified random split 80% train / 20% test; additional external holdout: all data from one study withheld (Ciofalo) for out‐of‐sample evaluation. Baselines: (1) empirical correlations (e.g., Re/Pr-based and We/d-based formulations), (2) pure data‐driven models: Decision Tree Regression (DTR), Random Forest Regression (RFR, n_estimators=400), Support Vector Regression (SVR, RBF), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP; 4 hidden layers: [128,128,64,32], lr=1e‐3), (3) gradient boosting (CatBoost, iterations=1000, lr=0.05). Physics‐augmented variants: same ML models trained to predict correction factor ξ where Nu_exp = Nu_cor × ξ and Nu_cor is the fitted general correlation. Correlation fitting: optimize coefficients/exponents of Nu_cor using Optuna (TPE) with 10,000 trials minimizing MAPE. Hyperparameter tuning: RandomizedSearchCV (5‐fold CV) or Bayesian optimization; random seeds fixed for reproducibility. Evaluation metrics: MAPE, RMSE, R2, SD, θ (fraction within ±30% MAPE), η (fraction within ±50% MAPE), prediction interval coverage (95%), calibration error, and applicability domain via Williams plot (leverage & standardized residuals). Uncertainty quantification: RFR Monte Carlo ensemble (100 varied seeds/models) and CatBoost quantile regression (0.025/0.975). Ablation studies: (A) physics feature ablation: compare models trained with vs without Nu_cor and with Nu_cor as multiplicative vs additive correction; (B) feature ablation: remove droplet dynamics (We, dd, um) to quantify sensitivity; (C) domain ablation: train on pressure‐atomizer subset and test on gas‐atomizer subset and vice versa. External validation: evaluate on withheld Ciofalo dataset and on per‐fluid leave‐one‐fluid‐out tests. Model interpretation: compute SHAP for global and local feature importance. Reporting: provide per‐model metric tables, confidence intervals, Williams plots, and SHAP explanations. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data coverage bias: consolidated dataset underrepresents extreme high‐pressure, very large/small nozzle diameters, and some nonaqueous fluids; models may mispredict outside trained ranges. Measurement uncertainty: droplet size and velocity measurements in source studies vary in accuracy and methodology, propagating label noise. Regime limitation: models are trained on non‐boiling conditions only and will not generalize to nucleate/film boiling regimes. Extrapolation risk: physics‐augmented correlation and ML may still fail when extrapolated far from training domain; applicability domain checks are necessary. Overfitting/transferability: deep models (MLP) risk overfitting given limited dataset size; generalization to new geometries (multi‐nozzle arrays, different target surface areas) is uncertain. Computational cost: large hyperparameter searches, Monte Carlo ensembles, and Optuna trials require significant compute resources. Interpretability limits: SHAP and post‐hoc explanations quantify importance but do not guarantee causal physical mechanisms. Uncertainty quantification limits: ensemble/quantile approaches capture some epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty but may underrepresent structural model error.
